query.explanation: `infer` declarations are only permitted inside the `extends` clause of a conditional type. `Unwrap` is fine, but `Holder` places `infer U` in an ordinary object type member, which the compiler rejects.
query.title: Where `infer` is allowed

questions.rationale: `Holder` uses `infer U` outside any conditional type's `extends` clause, which is an error, so the snippet does not compile cleanly.

choices.rationale: The tuple `[number, string]` has two elements, so it is not assignable to the empty tuple type `[]`.
`[unknown]` matches only one-element tuples; tuple lengths must agree, so a two-element tuple fails this check.
The final fallback is reached only when T matches none of the array checks, but a tuple is assignable to `unknown[]`.

query.explanation: Conditional types are evaluated top to bottom: the first branch whose check succeeds wins. `[number, string]` is not assignable to the empty tuple `[]`, and not to the one-element tuple `[unknown]` because tuple lengths must match. It is assignable to `unknown[]`, so the third branch is taken and `x` has type `"many"`.

query.title: Branch order in a nested conditional type

choices.rationale: `any` and `unknown` are mutually assignable, but conditional types are related only when their extends types are identical, which these are not.
Both branches union together only when the check type distributes over a union or is `any`; here the check type is a concrete function type.
Neither branch is `never` and the check type is not `never`, so the conditional always resolves to one of the two boolean literals.

query.explanation: When relating two conditional types, the compiler requires their check and extends types to be identical, not merely mutually assignable. `any` and `unknown` accept each other in normal assignments, but they are different types, so `T extends any ? 1 : 2` and `T extends unknown ? 1 : 2` are not identical and the outer check fails, giving `false`. This is exactly why the `Equal` trick can tell `any` apart from other types.
